summary: The MPLS Generic Associated Channel provides an auxiliary logical data channel for an LSP, pseudowire, or section, used for OAM and other protocols. This document defines a protocol to advertise which G-ACh capabilities are supported.

plainLanguage.summary: A side-channel on a network line carries helper messages. This lets devices announce which kinds of helper messages they understand.

questions: what is the mpls g-ach advertisement protocol
what is mpls g-ach channel type 0x0059
subtitle: A simple one-way protocol for MPLS devices to tell their peers about their capabilities and settings over the G-ACh.

tldr.problem: MPLS nodes often need basic information about the nodes at the other end of a link, LSP or pseudowire, but there was no link-layer-independent way to exchange it.
tldr.mechanism: The G-ACh Advertisement Protocol (GAP) sends messages over the Generic Associated Channel. Each message carries application-specific TLV objects with a lifetime, optionally protected by an HMAC-based authentication TLV.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can validate or adjust local configuration, and operators can diagnose faults and configuration mismatches. How a receiver uses the data is a local matter.

facts.label: TLV types
facts.value: 0 to 4 (Source Address, Request, Flush, Suppress, Authentication)

today: RFC 7212 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the protocol framework and the GAP's own TLVs, while other applications are defined in later documents.

sections.title: Why Advertise Over the G-ACh
sections.content:
The MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh, defined in RFC 5586) is an auxiliary logical data channel tied to an LSP, a pseudowire or a section (link). It is mostly used for OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) protocols such as BFD for MPLS and packet loss and delay measurement.

RFC 7212 defines how a Label Switching Router advertises its capabilities, configuration parameters or other application-specific information to peers over these channels. The guiding principle is simplicity: GAP is a one-way method of distributing information about the sender, and how a receiver uses it is a local matter.

The RFC compares the idea to LLDP on Ethernet. Unlike LLDP, GAP does not depend on the link-layer protocol, and it is not limited to adjacent nodes because the G-ACh exists for any LSP or pseudowire. One suggested use is discovering the Ethernet MAC addresses of MPLS-TP nodes that lack IP capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors on a street want to know what each other can do. GAP is a standard way to leave a note on the neighbor's porch, whatever kind of road connects you.

sections.title: How GAP Works in Brief
sections.content:
A device configured to send information for a data channel transmits GAP messages over the associated G-ACh. The payload is a collection of Type-Length-Value (TLV) objects, grouped per application, and an IANA registry identifies the applications. Application TLVs mostly carry static data the receiver keeps for a period of time.

A message can carry data for several applications, and a later message can refresh just some of them. In the RFC's example, a second message with data for application B leaves the receiver's data for applications A and C untouched. Messages are processed in the order received.

The sender chooses how often to send, and each application element carries a lifetime telling the receiver how long to keep the data. GAP has no fragmentation or reassembly, so applications must fragment their own data, and the application and operator must make sure GAP does not congest the link. GAP is designed for a unidirectional channel, and on a bidirectional channel a few receiver-to-sender messages are optional optimizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has labeled sections, one per topic. A new note about one topic only replaces that topic, and every section says how long it stays valid.

sections.title: Message and Element Formats
sections.content:
GAP uses Associated Channel Header channel type 0x0059, and the ACH is not followed by the ACH TLV header. Integers are in network byte order, reserved fields MUST be zero when sent and are ignored on receipt, and malformed messages MUST be discarded (an error MAY be logged, with rate limiting if logged remotely).

The message has a fixed header: a 4-bit Version (zero), 12 reserved bits, a 16-bit Message Length, a 32-bit Message Identifier and a 64-bit NTP Timestamp. The Message Identifier exists only for duplicate detection and MUST NOT be assumed to be a sequence number.

After the header comes the Application Data Block: one or more elements, each with a 16-bit Application ID, a 16-bit Element Length, a 16-bit Lifetime in seconds and then zero or more TLV objects. A lifetime of zero marks the data as immediately expired, and an element with no TLVs expires everything previously sent for that application. Each TLV has an 8-bit Type, 8 reserved bits and a 16-bit Length. GAP messages carry no checksum, so integrity needs the authentication TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note has a short cover sheet with a version, a size, an ID and the time it was written. Inside are labeled parts, each with its own expiry time.

sections.title: The Built-in GAP TLVs
sections.content:
GAP's own TLVs use Application ID 0x0000. They are metadata and instructions, not data to retain. If the GAP element is present it MUST come first in the message, and these messages MUST be processed in the order received.

  • Source Address (type 0): identifies the sender, with an address family and address. It SHOULD be included, and is REQUIRED on multipoint channels. In non-IP MPLS-TP networks it carries the channel endpoint identifier from RFC 6428.
  • GAP Request (type 1): asks the receiver to send an immediate unicast update, for all applications when the Length is zero, or for the listed Application IDs. It is meant for events such as a restart, and the reply is not guaranteed to cover every listed application.
  • GAP Flush (type 2): a null object telling the receiver to flush the data for all applications for this sender and channel. It does not apply to data in the same message.
  • GAP Suppress (type 3): asks the receiver to stop sending updates for a duration in seconds, for all applications or listed ones. The receiver MAY accept, ignore or resume at any time. A duration of zero cancels earlier requests.
  • GAP Authentication (type 4): carries a Key ID and authentication data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some notes are just instructions: who I am, tell me again, forget what I said, please stop sending for a while, and here is proof it was me.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
Sending and receiving operate per data channel and are configurable by the operator. Timers SHOULD be randomized across channels on an interface to avoid synchronized bursts. The Timestamp is the transmit time, and each element's Lifetime is the number of seconds the receiver should keep the data.

To keep data alive, a sender refreshes it, and refresh times SHOULD allow at least three updates before the Lifetime expires. The RFC's example is a Lifetime of 210 seconds with updates at least every 60 seconds. For extra reliability a sender MAY send several copies, such as three, and receivers can detect duplicates with the Message Identifier.

A receiver that cannot interpret an application's data MAY still keep it for its Lifetime, since it may help the operator. For data it understands, a new TLV of the same Type replaces the old one unless the application says otherwise. A receiver MAY use the data for auto-configuration, but that MUST be disabled by default and applications should avoid oscillation. Received data MUST be visible to operators, retained state MUST be discarded on restart, and all GAP applications MUST be disabled by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep sending your note again before it expires, a few times in a row to be safe. A neighbor who gets a note it cannot read may keep it anyway, because a human might find it useful.

sections.title: Message Authentication
sections.content:
Using GAP message authentication is RECOMMENDED. The sender adds an Authentication TLV whose data is a Message Authentication Code, an HMAC (RFC 2104) computed over the whole message with a secret key shared with the receiver. The procedure is based on IS-IS cryptographic authentication in RFC 5310.

A 16-bit Key ID names a set of parameters (algorithm and keystring) that are configured on both ends and never sent on the wire. HMAC-SHA-1 MUST be supported and HMAC-SHA-256 MAY be. The keystring SHOULD NOT be human-memorable, and implementers SHOULD consider RFC 7210 for key management. When computing the MAC the Authentication Data field is zeroed, and MAC truncation is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The receiver recomputes the MAC and discards the message if they differ. To stop replay attacks, the receiver compares the Timestamp with the current time within a reasonable tolerance, and clock corrections SHOULD be monotonic.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes are signed with a secret stamp only you and your neighbor know, so a fake note is spotted. The time on the note prevents someone from re-sending an old real one.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
GAP messages are sent in cleartext and no confidentiality is attempted, so GAP MUST NOT carry TLVs that need confidentiality, such as bare keying material. The more serious threat is forged or altered messages, which the authentication procedures and replay protection address.

When GAP is used for device discovery on a link, messages must be multicast. With the single G-ACh Label (value 13) the Ethernet destination address is 01-00-5e-80-00-0d.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes can be read by anyone nearby, so never put a secret in one. The stamp only protects against fakes.

fields.desc: Unique ID of the message, used for duplicate detection.
